application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Multi-processor execution platforms are being more and more commonly adopted in various real-time systems. In some systems, real-time tasks are generated at runtime to be executed under time constrains, e.g. interruptions triggered by events should be handled preemptively within their deadlines. Besides some other system verifications, checking whether all the real-time tasks can be finished within their deadlines, i.e. schedulability analysis is a very critical step in the design phase. In this paper, we break down a typical multi-processor real-time system into the follwing modules: the hardware environment, the task system, and the multi-processor execution platform. Then we develop a general model capturing the independent and interactive behaviors of these modules by modeling them as timed automata using the model-checking tool Uppaal, which enables us to perform formal verifications and schedulability analysis under one framework. We present verification results on small systems with a fairly small number of tasks and processors and it proves a general and flexible model which system designers can customize according to a certain system specification.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Multi-processor execution platforms are now being widely used due to the much higher computational power they provide compared to single processor platforms. For example, more and more embedded systems use multi-processor platforms to execute real-time applications partitioned into real-time tasks. Although systems can be designed in customized ways, an important problem has to be dealt with at the design phase of a system, that is to make sure all the tasks are finished within their deadlines, i.e. the schedulability analysis.

To perform schedulabilty analysis, traditional approach of schedulability tests based on processor utilization bounds is safe but pessimistic, furthermore, in some real-time systems, tasks can be generated sporadically and non-deterministically at runtime, e.g. systems with interrupts triggered by internal events, in this case, timed automata turn out to be more natural and powerful to model the release pattern and other behaviors of the tasks. In [15], [14], extended timed automata, task automata, are used specifically for schedulability analysis, there is much related research based on task automata and in [3], a tool has been developed based on the theory of task automata to do schedulability analysis on a single processor platform. When it comes to multi-processor platform, designers need to check the schedulability and other properties early in the design phase, a general methodology to model a system would come in handy if it can be easily and efficiently utilized to build the system model and enable designers to test the system in different scenarios.

In order to do that, we treat a typical multi-processor realtime system as a composition of these modules: the hardware environment, the task system, and the multi-processor execution platform. Hardware components interact with each other, and at the same time, non-deterministically generate tasks which are computed on different processors according to different scheduling principles. By breaking a system down this way, we can investigate each module's behaviors independently and see how they communicate and synchronously interact with each other, moreover, it's easy to see how small adjustments of one module affect the schedulability of the whole system. We leave interfaces within the model for designers to modify and thus making it a general and flexible model that can be customized according to a real life system specification. For example, for real-time applications running on multi-processor platform, tasks can be modeled as reoccurring periodic ones; for interrupts triggered by events, tasks can be easily modeled to be sporadically released from the environment. Each processor can adopt different scheduling principles, preemptively or non-preemptively.

div.head: Related work
div.p: The schedulability analysis of systems relates to the classical job-shop scheduling problem [5]. This problem is known to be NP-hard. The problem we are dealing with can be considered a generalization of the job-shop problem: we consider sporadic or cyclic tasks with best-case and worstcase execution times and preemptive scheduling principles. We will, however, just consider a decision version of the problem.

Schedulabilty analysis frequently needs to be done in realtime system designs, the notion of tasks naturally relates to interrupts triggered by events in the system that need to be handled. [12] discusses a situation where there exist nested interrupts in a real-time system, and an urgent interrupt is allowed to preempt the current interrupt handling, a compositional model is proposed to analyze the scheduling of nested interrupts. Then, following the work in [12], a model controller automata is proposed in [13] to handle behaviors and interactions of real-time systems with mutex components. Our model in this paper provides a way of handling interrupts on multi-processor platforms.

Modeling and verification of real-time systems are approached in a simulation manner or a formal manner. The advantage of simulation methodologies is that the designers, early in the development process, receive feedback on the feasibility of the chosen designs before they are implemented. The simulation approaches do, however, not cover all critical cases or give any guarantee of the inexistence of errors like missed deadlines or memory overflow.

Several formal approaches have been proposed to handle the drawbacks of simulation approaches. [1] provides a real-time calculus for scheduling of preemptive tasks, but it's limited to static priority scheduling. In [2], a timed automata approach for schedulability analysis of single processor systems is provided, and it is shown that the schedulability problem for extended timed automata is decidable for preemptive scheduling strategies. This approach is also applied in the Times tool [3] which analyzes schedulability of tasks on a single processor only. As shown in [6], [7], the timed automata model is a very natural tool for modeling and solving scheduling problems in general. So, like the TIMES tool, our approach is also based on a timed automata model but in a multiprocessor setting. And our work is based on the positive decidability conclusion shown in [4] that the schedulability analysis problem is decidable for multi-processor systems with non-preemptive schedulers or tasks with fixed execution times.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: in Section 2, we present the basis of our work: the timed automata theory and the Uppaal tool introduction. In Section 3, a system model is depicted, and we describe three main sub modules and give their timed automata implementations within Uppaal respectively. Experimental results are presented in Section 4. The last section is the conclusion.

div.head: II. PRELIMINARIES
div.p: Timed Automata is a theory for modeling and verification of real-time systems. In the original theory of timed automata [8], a timed automaton is a finite-state Büchi automaton extended with a set of real-valued variables modeling clocks. Constraints on the clock variables are used to restrict the behavior of an automaton, and Büchi accepting conditions are used to enforce progress properties. Then timed safety automata [11] is introduced to specify progress properties using local invariant conditions. Due to its simplicity, timed safety automata has been adopted in several verification tools for timed automata, e.g. UPPAAL [9], [10] is a toolbox for verification of real-time systems jointly developed by Uppsala University and Aalborg University. In this paper, we shall focus on timed safety automata, and refer to them as timed automata or simply automata.
This section serves as a brief review on the timed automata theory and Uppaal.

div.head: B. The Uppaal tool
div.p: The model-checker Uppaal [9], [10] is based on the theory of timed automata and its modelling language offers additional features such as bounded integer variables and urgency. The query language of Uppaal, used to specify properties to be checked, is a subset of CTL (computation tree logic).

Timed automata are often composed into a network of timed automata over a common set of clocks and actions, consisting of n timed automata 𝐴 𝑖 = (𝐸, 𝐻, 𝑄 𝑖 , 𝑞 0 𝑖 , 𝑋, 𝐼 𝑖 , 𝛿 𝑖 ), 1 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑛. A location vector is a vector q = (𝑞 1 , . . . , 𝑞 𝑛 ). We compose the invariant functions into a common function over location vectors 𝐼(q) = ∧ 𝑖 𝐼 𝑖 (𝑞 𝑖 ). We write q[𝑞 ′ 𝑖 /𝑞 𝑖 ] to denote the vector where the 𝑖th element 𝑞 𝑖 of q is replaced by 𝑞 ′ 𝑖 . In the following we define the semantics of a network of timed automata.

1) Definition 4: (Semantics of a network of TA). Let 𝐴 𝑖 = (𝐸, 𝐻, 𝑄 𝑖 , 𝑞 0 𝑖 , 𝑋, 𝐼 𝑖 , 𝛿 𝑖 ) be a network of n timed automata. Let q0 = (𝑞 0 1 , . . . , 𝑞 0 𝑛 ) be the initial location vector. A configuration of a network of TA is a pair (q, 𝜈) of a location vector q = (𝑞 1 , . . . , 𝑞 𝑛 ), and a clock valuation 𝜈 on 𝑋. The labeled transition system is as follows:

div.p: Uppaal [9], [10] uses a simplified version of CTL, the query language consists of path formulae and state formulae. State formulae describe individual states, path formulae quantify over paths or traces of the model. Path formulae can be classified into reachability, safety and liveness. Next, we use Uppaal to do modeling and verifications.

div.head: III. THE SYSTEM FRAMEWORK OVERVIEW
div.p: A multi-processor real-time system can generally be designed as a composition of three modules: the hardware environment, the task system, and the multi-processor execution platform. The hardware environment represents the hardware configuration of the system, system components can interact with each other, meanwhile, the environment can trigger a realtime task to be computed. A task system is a set of real-time tasks, each of the tasks may have its own characteristics described by a set of parameters such as release pattern(sporadic or periodic), best and worst-case execution times, deadline, priority, etc. Tasks are computed on the execution platform made up of multiple processors each capable of executing tasks according to a given scheduling principle.

A multi-processor system should be considered as a whole, so we try to build a model that comprises the three modules and meanwhile exhibits the parallel activities and interactions occurring within the system. Since the time constrained behaviors are naturally modeled by clocks and timed automata, and Uppaal has proven to be a successful model-checking tool based on timed automata, so we use Uppaal for modeling, verification and simulation. We are dealing with preemptive scheduling which means the running time of a task should be temporarily stopped when the task is preempted by another task, but Uppaal does not support stopwatches for now, and for the simplicity of presentation and comprehension, we make the execution time in the Uppaal model discrete. Other clocks still operate continuously.

Following is a top-down description of the timed-automata model of the system framework, where a system is described as a parallel composition of the three modules: System = the environment ∥ the task system ∥ the execution platform The environment = ∥ 𝜔∈Ω 𝑇 𝐴(𝜔)
The task system = ∥ 𝜏 ∈Γ 𝑇 𝐴(𝜏 )

The execution platform = ∥ 𝑀 𝑗=1 𝑇 𝐴(𝑝𝑒 𝑗 ) Where ∥ denotes parallel composition of timed automata. Ω is the set of environment components ranged over by 𝜔, Γ is the set of tasks ranged over by 𝜏 and a execution platform is made up of M processors denoted by pe. Thus, the environment is just the parallel composition of the timed automata of the components; the task system consists of a collection of timed automata for tasks combined in parallel; the execution platform consists of a parallel composition of timed automata for processors.
Next, we give each module a more detailed description and an implementation in Uppaal.

div.head: A. The environment
div.p: The environment module represents the hardware components communicating and synchronously interacting with each other in the system, and we always need to make sure that they show desired properties and to detect subtle errors early in the design phase. Using timed automata in modeling the environment, one may specify general timing constraints and model other behavioral aspects such as concurrency and synchronization. Sometimes, environment components show external behaviors besides just interacting internally, e.g. in an interrupt handling system, whenever an interrupt signal occurs, the associated interrupt handling program will be executed. If we treat each interrupt program as a task, the environment is also viewed as a generator that releases the tasks system. In Uppaal model, we associate each task with an action channel, whenever a synchronization happens on the action channel, the task is released. Thus, the sporadic release pattern of the tasks is modeled naturally together with the time constrained behavior of the environment.

Different systems have their own environments, what the specific environment looks like does not matter as we are demonstrating how the environment generates the task system. So we choose an example presented in [9] as our environment to help us illustrate and we do some modifications on it, e.g. we declare a channel 𝑎𝑝𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑢𝑝𝑡[𝑖] for every task, whenever one train is trying to approach the bridge, it will release a synchronization message to the Gate controller and immediately trigger a task to be handled via the respective apprinterupt channel. div.head: B. The task system
div.p: Let Γ denote a finite set of tasks. Each task 𝜏 ∈ Γ is characterized by a deadline 𝑑 ∈ ℕ, a best-case execution time 𝑏𝑐𝑒𝑡 𝜏 ∈ ℕ and a worst-case execution time 𝑤𝑐𝑒𝑡 𝜏 ∈ ℕ, where 𝑑 > 𝑤𝑐𝑒𝑡 𝜏 ≥ 𝑏𝑐𝑒𝑡 𝜏 > 0. In a given run, a task's execution time 𝑒 ∈ ℕ is a certain amount of time units of a processor's time which is bounded within the range [𝑏𝑐𝑒𝑡 𝜏 , 𝑤𝑐𝑒𝑡 𝜏 ]. The execution platform consists of 𝑀 processors each denoted by 𝑝𝑒 𝑖 , and there exists a mapping 𝑚 : Γ → {1, . . . , 𝑀} of tasks to processors, we often consider the set of tasks Γ 𝑝𝑒𝑖 mapped to a particular processor 𝑝𝑒 𝑖 , i.e. let Γ 𝑝𝑒𝑖 = 𝑚 -1 (𝑖) = {𝜏 ∈ Γ | 𝑚(𝜏 ) = 𝑖}. Suppose that the set of tasks Γ 𝑝𝑒𝑖 = {𝜏 𝑖1 , . . . , 𝜏 𝑖 𝑘 } is executed on the processor 𝑝𝑒 𝑖 . The timed automata for these 𝑘 tasks and the processor 𝑝𝑒 𝑖 share four channels 𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦 𝑖 , 𝑟𝑢𝑛 𝑖 , 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑚𝑝𝑡 𝑖 and 𝑓 𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑠ℎ 𝑖 . Now we present the timed automaton 𝑇 𝐴(𝜏 ) for a task 𝜏 ∈ Γ 𝑝𝑒𝑖 with deadline d and best-case and worst-case execution times 𝑏𝑐𝑒𝑡(bcet) and 𝑤𝑐𝑒𝑡(wcet). The timed automaton implemented in Uppaal can be seen in Fig. 2.

A clock at(accumulated time) is used to record the time elapsed after the task is released, from it, we can tell how much time is left before the deadline. The timed automaton stays in the Done location until it receives a triggering message from an approaching train.

In the Done location, the task has finished its job in the current run and is waiting the start of the next, where the transition from ReadytoRelease to Waiting is taken. This is signalled to the processor 𝑝𝑒 𝑖 using the channel 𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦 𝑖 . The local integer pe indicates which processor the task is executed on. In this transition the clock at and other variables are initialized. In particular, a choice is taken setting e nondeterministically to a value in {𝑏𝑐𝑒𝑡, 𝑏𝑐𝑒𝑡 + 1, . . . , 𝑤𝑐𝑒𝑡}. Furthermore, the integer variable cr holds the execution time for 𝜏 in the current run and is initialized to 0. Now Uppaal doesn't support stopwatch, but we have preemptive scheduling and we cannot use a clock to hold the execution time for 𝜏 in the current run, therefore, we have to introduce the integer variable cr and update it in discrete steps as described in the following.

The transition from Waiting to Running takes place when the processing element 𝑝𝑒 𝑖 sends a signal on the 𝑟𝑢𝑛 𝑖 channel to the task. This transition takes place when the task is enabled and has highest priority among the enabled tasks on 𝑝𝑒 𝑖 . On this transition, the clock x, which is used to record one time unit, is set to 0. In one round from state Running via Discrete and back to Running the effect is that one time unit has elapsed and that the running time cr is incremented by 1.

Transitions from Waiting and Discrete to MissedDeadline are taken when a deadline is missed. Furthermore, a transition from Running to Done is taken when the task has finished its job in the current run 𝑐𝑟 == 𝑒 and this is signalled to the processor 𝑝𝑒 𝑖 by a 𝑓 𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑠ℎ 𝑖 event. Since cr is not a clock we ensure that the transition is taken without delay by making the finish channels urgent. In the Running location, the task may be preempted when a task on 𝑝𝑒 𝑖 with higher priority becomes enabled. In this case the processor issues a 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑚𝑝𝑡 𝑖 signal and the task makes a transition to the Waiting state.

Communication between the processors and the tasks is done over the synchronization channels ready, run, preempt and finish. Some of this communication requires value transfer in order to identify the task in question because all tasks on a given processor share the same channels. The global array tauid is used so that 𝑡𝑎𝑢𝑖𝑑[𝑖 -1] handles the communication on 𝑝𝑒 𝑖 .

In order to avoid some undesired behavior, two locking mechanisms are used. One locking mechanism implemented by the array disc and the boolean function lockT makes sure that all tasks are able to react when a preempt signal can occur, i.e. they are in the Running location. The other locking mechanism implemented by the array taskFinishing and the boolean function lockPE makes sure that all finish signals are reacted to by the platform before any ready signals can be handled. This is done in order not to preempt a task that has actually just finished. These two locking mechanisms ensure the absence of deadlocks mentioned above.

div.head: Fig. 3. The processor timed automaton template
div.p: The task template can be easily modified to model periodic tasks by just changing 𝑑𝑙[𝑇 ] to 𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑖𝑜𝑑[𝑇 ] that records each task's period and changing the release of tasks to a reoccurring fashion.

div.head: C. The execution platform
div.p: A platform is made up of M processors 𝑝𝑒 𝑖 , 1 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑀 , where each processing element 𝑝𝑒 𝑖 is capable of executing tasks according to a given scheduling principle. We will here consider the following preemptive scheduling strategies: ratemonotonic RM, fixed-priority FP and earliest-deadline-first EDF scheduling. There will be no principal difficulties in extending the model with more scheduling principles, but this will, of course, add more details.
A task 𝜏 has higher fixed priority than 𝜏 ′ , written 𝜏 > 𝑓𝑝 𝜏 ′ , iff 𝑝𝑟(𝜏 ) < 𝑝𝑟(𝜏 ′ ), i.e. smaller number given by pr means higher priority.

For rate-monotonic scheduling, the priority relation among tasks is primarily given by their periods (shorter period means higher priority) and secondarily by their numbering according to pr: A task 𝜏 has higher rate-monotonic priority than 𝜏

Each processor can schedule its assigned tasks according to a given scheduling discipline, and this can be customized within the Uppaal model of the processor by the designers. The processor template implemented in Uppaal can be seen in Fig. 3.

The main idea is that the processor in the initial location Start, can react to signals ready! and finish! from its own tasks. On such events it enters the scheduling status to decide which task should be chosen to execute and before reentering the Start location it issues the necessary preempt and run signals to its own tasks.

Notice that time does not progress in one round from the Start location and back, as all other locations of the processor are committed or urgent. The single urgent location is used to capture all finish signals available at that point in time.

Each processor maintains arrays describing the tasks that are currently released(waiting), enabled(waiting or running) and executing, aTaskIsReady and Running are boolean flags indicating whether there is a task waiting to run and the processor is now occupied.

After the task is ReadyForScheduling, the procedure tasksReadyOnProc initiates the scheduling decision making by finding a task that is enabled, and setting aTaskIsReady to true. If no tasks on the processor are waiting, aTaskIsReady is set to false.

The procedure findHighestPriority finds the enabled task with the highest priority on the processor based on the scheduling discipline chosen and sets selected to the number of that task. Specific scheduling principles are implemented within the body of this function, and designers can choose among the three principles whose definitions we've given at the beginning of this section. The static scheduling disciplines (fixed priority and rate monotonic) implementations are straightforward so it's our choice in this system.

After coming to the selection a task to execute, the processor inform the task via sending the run! message, if a task needs to be preempted first, the processor preempts it and then returns back to the Start location.

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: In this section, we use the model checking tool Uppaal to perform the schedulability analysis and some formal verifications. In the first case, we make the environment consist of four trains and one bridge controller, each train is related to a corresponding task, and there are four kinds of tasks which are computed on a platform made up of two processors. The mapping of tasks is implemented by the array 𝑚𝑎𝑝[𝑇 ] with 𝑇 denoting the number of tasks. We use global arrays 𝑑𝑙[𝑇 ], 𝑏𝑐𝑒𝑡[𝑇 ], 𝑤𝑐𝑒𝑡[𝑇 ] to specify each task's parameters: deadline d, best-case-execution time bcet, worst-case-execution time wcet. In this case,

We set the deadlines all to 13, because it takes at least 13 time units for one train to cross the bridge and come back to approach the bridge again, and we need the related task to complete within at most 13 time units in order to handle the interrupt triggered by the train's approaching.
We are interested to know whether the system satisfies some desired properties. So first, we perform the following checking:
• 𝐸 <> Train(1).Stop && Train(2).Stop && Train(3).Stop && Train(4).Cross
div.formula: • 𝐴[] Gate.list[𝑁 ] == 0 • 𝐴[] not deadlock • 𝐴[]
div.p: forall (𝑖:idt) forall (𝑗:idt) Train(𝑖).Cross && Train(𝑗).Cross imply 𝑖 == 𝑗 We issue the above properties because we want to ensure that some train, e.g. train(4), can be crossing the bridge while other trains are stopped; there can never be N elements in the queue (thus the queue of the bridge controller will not overflow); the system is deadlock-free; there is never more than one train crossing the bridge at any time instance. These are just examples of verifications making sure the system especially the environment is correctly designed as desired. The properties are all satisfied. Now we move on to schedulability checking, we use static scheduling principle(FP) for both processors and we issue the queries:
div.formula: 𝐸 <> task1.MissedDeadline ∥ task2.MissedDeadline ∥ task3.MissedDeadline ∥ task4.MissedDeadline • 𝐸 <> task1.MissedDeadline • 𝐸 <> task2.MissedDeadline • 𝐸 <> task3.MissedDeadline • 𝐸 <> task4.MissedDeadline
div.p: These queries are used to find out if the system is schedulable. If the first property is not satisfied, it means that the system is schedulable, if it's not the case, the system is not schedulable and we can identify which task misses its deadline using the next four properties. In this case, the system is schedulable.

But, if we change the specifications of the tasks to 𝑚𝑎𝑝[𝑇 ] = {1, 1, 2, 2}, 𝑑𝑙[𝑇 ] = {13, 13, 13, 13}, 𝑏𝑐𝑒𝑡[𝑇 ] = {4, 6, 6, 6}, 𝑤𝑐𝑒𝑡[𝑇 ] = {4, 6, 6, 6}. The system is NOT schedulable since task4 misses its deadline(the property 𝐸 <> task4. MissedDeadline is satisfied). The Uppaal system can generate a diagnostic trace for this and it's a very useful for understanding the scenario where a deadline is missed, from the trace, you can see which task is executing on which processor at each time unit and how a task ends up missing its deadline. It is easy to explore various designs using this model and, for example, changing the scheduling principle on processor2 to earliest deadline first will give a schedulable system.

Until now, we've done the schedulability analysis and formal verification using the model, and we have tested the model on a collection of task examples and the verifications gave correct results, so it proves to be feasible as a general model for designers when it comes to multi-processor realtime system designing and schedulability analysis.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: We have developed a general model for typical multiprocessor real-time systems composed by three modules, analysis of such systems could be quite complicated due to the various choices made concerning the specifications of each of these modules early at the design phase, so we make the timed automata implementations of these modules in the Uppaal system allow us to investigate each module's internal behaviors independently and their synchronous interactions from a system level view.

We have presented experimental results on rather small systems with high complexity, primarily due to differences between best-case and worst-case execution times. By considering worst-case execution times only, where the system becomes deterministic, we then carry out experiments on a collection of small systems with limited number of tasks and processors, and the positive results show that the model we present can be used as a general and flexible model that designers can customize according to the real systems under consideration.

In the future, we'll try to extend our model to introduce other costs such as memory and power usage besides timing. Furthermore, we used the discrete execution model in our timed automata implementations which are not as efficient and precise as those using stopwatches, so future experiments using stopwatches give hope to decrease the memory consumption as well as verification time.
